Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow. Piet Mondrian's 1921 geometric abstraction comprises primary colors, black lines, and white fields arranged in a grid, a quintessential work of De Stijl that distills painting to its mathematical essence. It represents the radical elimination of representation in favor of pure formal harmony and universal visual order.

Painted in 1921, it was created during Mondrian's mature period after he founded the De Stijl movement with fellow Dutch artists in 1917. The composition consists entirely of rectangular fields bounded by thick black lines and filled with primary colors—red, blue, yellow—plus black and white in careful asymmetrical balance. Mondrian eliminated all reference to nature, objects, or emotion, instead pursuing a utopian vision of universal harmony through geometric reduction and primary colors.

Mondrian believed this formal vocabulary could express underlying spiritual truths and transcend individual subjectivity, influencing architecture, design, and ideology. Works in this series vary in proportion and color distribution, yet each maintains the same vocabulary of grid, line, primary color, and void. The painting exemplifies the De Stijl philosophy: abstraction, geometric rigor, and the integration of art into all aspects of modern life and design.
